title: DNS Resolution
summary: DNS turns names like www.example.com into IP addresses using a global, delegated hierarchy. Your device asks a recursive resolver, which walks down from the root servers to the .com servers to the domain's own authoritative servers, following referrals. Every answer carries a TTL, and heavy caching at each layer is what lets a system answering trillions of queries a day respond in milliseconds.

walkthrough.title: Ask the resolver
walkthrough.text: The browser's OS stub resolver asks the configured recursive resolver (ISP, 1.1.1.1, or 8.8.8.8) for the A record of www.example.com. If a fresh copy is cached, it answers immediately.

walkthrough.title: Ask a root server
walkthrough.text: On a cache miss, the resolver asks one of the 13 root server identities, each served from hundreds of anycast sites. The root does not know the answer but refers it to the .com name servers.

walkthrough.title: Ask the TLD server
walkthrough.text: The .com servers refer it to example.com's authoritative name servers (ns1.example-dns.net), including their IP addresses as 'glue' when needed.

walkthrough.title: Ask the authoritative server
walkthrough.text: The authoritative server returns the answer, www → 93.184.216.34 with TTL 300. With DNSSEC, the resolver also checks the chain of signatures from the root down.

walkthrough.title: Cache and answer
walkthrough.text: The resolver caches every answer and referral for its TTL, so the next million users skip most of these steps, then returns the IP to the client.

walkthrough.title: Change a record
walkthrough.text: The domain owner updates the record through their DNS provider. The change is live on the authoritative servers in seconds, but resolvers keep serving the old value until their cached TTL runs out. That waiting period is what people call 'propagation'.

data.label: Device (Stub Resolver)
responsibilities: Sends every lookup to one configured recursive resolver.
Keeps a small local cache honouring TTLs.
Can encrypt queries with DNS-over-HTTPS or DNS-over-TLS.

failureModes.impact: 'The internet is down' even though the network works.
failureModes.mitigation: Configure two resolvers on different networks.
DoH/DoT to a trusted resolver; DNSSEC validation.

data.label: Recursive Resolver

output.name: Iterative queries
output.type: To root → TLD → authoritative on a miss

responsibilities: Does the work of walking the hierarchy for its clients.
Caches answers and referrals until their TTLs expire.
Validates DNSSEC signatures and randomises query IDs and ports.

failureModes.impact: Users sent to an attacker's IP.
failureModes.mitigation: Random source ports and IDs, DNSSEC validation, 0x20 case randomisation.

failureModes.scenario: Authoritative server for a popular domain down
failureModes.impact: Lookups fail once cached entries expire.
failureModes.mitigation: Serve-stale: return expired answers briefly while retrying.

data.label: Root Servers
responsibilities: Knows which servers are authoritative for each top-level domain.
Signs the root zone, the DNSSEC trust anchor.
Is rarely queried because referrals are cached for days.

failureModes.impact: In theory, resolution of new TLD lookups fails.
failureModes.mitigation: Massive anycast spread; long-cached TLD referrals make users barely notice.

failureModes.impact: Validating resolvers with stale trust anchors fail.
failureModes.mitigation: Automated trust-anchor updates (RFC 5011) and long transition periods.

data.label: TLD Servers (.com)

output.name: Referral
output.type: NS ns1.example-dns.net + glue IPs, DS record

responsibilities: Delegates each registered domain to its name servers.
Publishes DS records that link the domain into the DNSSEC chain.
Updates when owners change name servers at their registrar.

failureModes.scenario: Wrong NS set at the registrar
failureModes.impact: Entire domain unresolvable for its TTL (often 2 days).
failureModes.mitigation: Double-check NS changes; keep old servers answering during migration.

failureModes.scenario: Stale DS record after changing DNS provider
failureModes.impact: DNSSEC validation fails and the domain disappears for validating users.
failureModes.mitigation: Follow the DNSSEC key rollover steps when moving providers.

data.label: Authoritative Servers
responsibilities: Holds the source of truth for the domain's records.
Can answer differently by location or health (GeoDNS, failover).

failureModes.impact: Major sites unreachable once caches expire.
failureModes.mitigation: Two independent providers serving the same zone.

failureModes.scenario: TTL too long before a migration
failureModes.impact: The cutover takes days to reach everyone.
failureModes.mitigation: Lower TTLs a day or two ahead of planned changes.

data.label: Zone Management

output.name: Zone update
output.type: Pushed to all authoritative PoPs in seconds

responsibilities: Manages records as code with review.
Pushes changes to every authoritative location.
Keeps multiple providers' zones in sync.

failureModes.mitigation: Changes via reviewed code, plans that show deletions, and zone backups.

failureModes.scenario: Dangling CNAME to a deprovisioned resource
failureModes.mitigation: Remove records when resources are deleted; scan for dangling entries.
